titleStmt.title: To Harriet Shaw Weaver. Sunday, 18 March 1923
titleStmt.author: James Joyce

seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: I am dictating this to my son because on Tuesday I got sudden flare up in the eye, and have been in pain but must most of all in dread lest it should turn to iritis. But to-day sixt sixth day it is still confined to the conjunctiva and Dr Borsch thinks iritis most improbable. The curious thing is, that even yesterday while the outer eye was all inflamed the dionine was still clearing up the film and the pupil. The doctor said: Your eye is as puzzling as the money market. So it is, and as ruinous.

This morning I am better and had a good rest. I spent several sleepless nights partly in fear and partly wrighting writing
wich which I dictated the next morning. The pages you call historic will be of course yours with the manuscript when and if ever completed. The passage is towards the end of the book, but only the brieff brief draft written without nots notes .

I dreamed last night that Mr Quinn was hanged. This should mean some honor honour for him, which I hope he will get as he hase has done many things for me. Thank you for the Tribuna. Did Mr Cecchi get a press copy? If not perhaps one could be spared as his second article may hasten Mr Debosis de Bosis’s
plans.
I shall dictate a letter in a few days about the Hamlet episode.

It seems to me that Mr Darrantiére Darantiere
should demand the restitution of
dose those copies. So sequestration seems to me quite illegal.

div.note: Despite JJ’s ongoing ocular ailments, Dr Borsch reassured him that he did not have glaucoma and (as JJ had written to Weaver on 11 March 1923) “said too that I did well not to be operated in London, that my sight had resisted marvellously and that I am quite healthy!!!” (LI 201). Borsch would not operate on JJ’s eyes until April 1923.
JJ had begun dionine treatment for his eyes with Dr Louis Colin during his holiday in Nice in the autumn of 1922 (JJ 537-38).

A week earlier (11 March 1923), JJ had written to Weaver: “Yesterday I wrote two pages – the first I have written since the final Yes of Ulysses” (LI 202). That was the Roderick O’Conor sketch (BM 47480-267r). On the verso, he partially wrote the first draft of a sketch known as the kiss of Tristan and Isolde, written on two folios which, at some point, were separated: one folio is now at the National Library of Ireland (NLI MS 41,818, f. 1) and one – the back of the Roderick O’Conor sketch – at the British Library (BL 47480-267v). In this sketch, Tristan recites JJ’s own lyrical poetry – “Night Piece”, partially published in Poetry magazine (10, no. 2 [May 1917], 74), and later published in Pomes Penyeach). In 1923, JJ’s plan for what would become Finnegans Wake placed this passage towards the end of the book. Later, it became the starting point of Book II, chapter 4 of Finnegans Wake.

The Italian literary critic Emilio Cecchi published a review of Ulysses in La Tribuna on 2 March 1923. JJ wrote to Weaver on 11 March 1923, “Would it be too much to ask you to send me registered the copy of La Tribuna with the article by Mr Cecchi as I am sceptical about the arrival of another copy” (LI 201).

In a letter to Weaver on 30 December 1922, JJ had written of the possibility of “an Italian edition of Ulysses exactly similar to Larbaud’s, to be published by Stock of Rome” and requested a press copy to be sent to Lauro de Bosis. In a letter sent to Cecchi on 2 April 1923, JJ enquired about his second article on Ulysses for Il Convegno. Cecchi’s second article does not appear to have been published (LIII 75).
500 copies of the second Egoist Press edition of Ulysses published in January 1923 were seized by English customs authorities at Folkestone (LI 201).
The signature is in JJ’s hand, not in Giorgio’s.
